Half Area Of Quadrilateral

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: the line from C to E cuts the four-sided shape into two parts of the same size.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick names, premise and hint to see how the line is found.
Look for the math

Drag a corner and the two coloured pieces change shape, yet they keep the same size. The construction has only three steps, and a short chain of equal triangle areas explains why.

Finding E

B is joined to D, and K = (B + D) / 2 is the midpoint of that diagonal. Through K, draw the line parallel to the other diagonal AC. It meets AB or AD (whichever is nearer) at E. The applet draws KE and the dividing line CE when you tick premise. The original problem assumes E falls on AB; the applet also lets it fall on AD. The page embeds two copies of the original, one with the point names hidden and one with them shown; the names checkbox here starts shown.

Equal triangles, equal halves

Because K halves BD, triangles ABK and ADK share an altitude from A and have equal bases, so their areas match; the same is true of CBK and CDK. Therefore the two quadrilaterals ABCK and ADCK have equal area. Since KE is parallel to AC, triangles AEK and CEK share the base EK and the same altitude between the parallels, so they match too. Let L be where AK crosses CE: removing the common triangle LEK leaves AEL and CKL with equal area.

The final swap

Starting from ABCK, replace AEL by CKL and you get triangle BCE. Starting from ADCK, replace CKL by AEL and you get AECD. Both starting pieces were equal and both swaps moved the same area, so area(BCE) = area(AECD): CE halves the quadrilateral. Tick hint to see the two triangles AEK and CEK and the crossing L that make this swap visible.

What the checks found

The logic test measured both pieces with an independent shoelace formula on the applet's own construction: the start shape, a square, a rectangle, a dart, a crossed shape, a 48-by-48 grid of corner positions and four thousand random shapes. The two areas agreed everywhere, including every concave case where BD lies inside the shape, exactly as the page states. The nearer crossing also always landed on AB or AD. When BD lies outside the shape the polygon areas still match, but CE need not split the drawing into two pieces, so the page's caveat matters. In a parallelogram-like case E is A itself and L is not a separate point; the diagonal still halves the shape, though the last triangle swap degenerates. This is different from Dividing Evenly a Quadrilateral II: that applet draws a parallel through B or D, takes the median from C to the midpoint M, and bisects with CM instead of CE.

Tick premise, then drag C until E jumps from AB to AD: watch the equality survive the jump.
